title: Language level lab
mission: Compare high-level, assembly and machine code, then justify a language choice for a project.
donow: Why might two programmers choose different languages to solve the same problem?
outcomes: Distinguish source code, assembly and machine code.
Justify language choices using project requirements.
starter: A school needs a quiz app that staff can update. A device needs precise control of processor registers. Would the same language level suit both equally well? Explain.
starter_answer: The quiz may suit a high-level language because readable code is easier to maintain. The hardware routine may suit a low-level language because it exposes processor operations.
terms: High-level language
A language that abstracts many hardware details using human-readable constructs.
Low-level language
A language closely related to a processor instruction set and hardware operations.

stations.name: High-level languages
facts: Use readable words and familiar operations to express a solution.
Hide many details of how the processor works.
Usually easier to write, understand and maintain.
stations.challenge: Why might a school choose Python to build a quiz?

tasks.q: What makes a language high-level?
a: It hides many hardware details behind readable instructions
It can only run on a powerful computer
It is always faster than every other language
tasks.fb: High-level describes the level of abstraction, not the speed or quality of the computer.

tasks.q: The Python example calculates 4 + 7. What does print(total) output?
tasks.fb: Both values are numbers. The addition produces 11, which is stored in total and then displayed.

stations.answer: Python hides hardware details and is readable, so staff can build and maintain the quiz more easily.
stations.info: Language level alone does not decide speed. The algorithm, translator, implementation and hardware all matter.

stations.name: Low-level languages
facts: Close to the instructions and hardware of a processor.
Machine code and assembly are low-level languages.
Offer detailed control, but are harder to write and maintain.
stations.challenge: Why might precise hardware control matter in a device?

tasks.q: Which level is each characteristic most closely associated with?
items: Usually easier for people to maintain
Closely tied to a processor instruction set
tasks.fb: High-level languages prioritise abstraction and readability. Low-level languages expose more hardware detail.

tasks.q: A programmer needs precise control of processor registers. Which is the stronger reason to consider a low-level language?
a: It exposes hardware operations more directly
It guarantees there will be no bugs
It runs unchanged on every processor
It is always quicker to develop
tasks.fb: Choose a language for the task requirements. Low-level code gives control, not a guarantee of correctness.

stations.answer: A device may need exact control over processor operations or memory use. Low-level code exposes these details.
stations.info: More control can mean more code and more details to manage. Development time and testing effort still matter.

stations.name: Machine code
facts: Binary instructions that a compatible CPU can execute.
Each processor family has its own instruction set.
Difficult for people to read, write and check directly.
stations.challenge: Would the same machine code work on every CPU? Explain.

tasks.q: Which form of program instruction can a CPU execute directly?
a: Machine code for its instruction set
tasks.fb: A CPU executes machine instructions it recognises. Human-readable source code must be translated.

tasks.q: Select TWO accurate statements about machine code.
opts: Instructions are represented in binary
The instruction set matters
Every CPU understands the same instructions
It is usually easier to maintain than high-level code
tasks.fb: Machine code is binary and specific to a compatible instruction set. A string of bits has no universal instruction meaning.

stations.answer: No. A CPU must support the instruction set used by that machine code.
stations.info: The binary diagram is illustrative. Actual instruction lengths and encodings depend on the processor architecture.

stations.name: Assembly language
facts: Uses short instruction names called mnemonics.
Closely follows a particular processor instruction set.
Easier to read than binary, but still needs translation.
stations.challenge: Why is assembly low-level even though it uses words?

tasks.q: Match the description to the correct term.
pairs: Short instruction names such as ADD
Binary instructions executed by a CPU
tasks.fb: Assembly is source code too. It uses mnemonic instructions but remains close to the processor.

tasks.q: A simplified example loads 4 into R0, then adds 7 to R0. What value is now in R0?
tasks.fb: The register first holds 4. Adding 7 changes it to 11. This is an illustrative instruction model, not a specific processor syntax.

stations.answer: Assembly instructions remain closely tied to a processor instruction set, even though mnemonics are readable.
stations.info: The register example shows the idea of assembly. You do not need to learn these illustrative instructions for OCR J277.

stations.name: Moving between devices
facts: High-level source is often more portable between systems.
A suitable translator or runtime must be available.
Low-level code may need rewriting for another instruction set.
stations.challenge: What must be available before a Python program can run on a new computer?

tasks.q: What does portable source code mean?
a: It can be used on different systems with suitable supporting software
Its file is always small enough for a memory stick
It requires no translation on any computer
It works without an operating system
tasks.fb: Portability is about using code across systems. It still depends on suitable software and any required libraries.

tasks.q: Does each statement about portability hold?
items: Python source needs a suitable runtime on the new system
Every machine-code program runs on every CPU
Hardware-specific code may need changes on a new processor
High-level code can depend on libraries that must also be available
tasks.fb: High-level code is often more portable, but the runtime, libraries and system features must still be compatible.

stations.answer: A compatible Python runtime and any required libraries must be available.
stations.info: Portable source code and a portable executable are different ideas. Reusing source may require translating it for the target system.

stations.name: Choosing the right level
facts: Match the language to the requirements of the project.
High-level code can reduce development and maintenance effort.
Low-level code can provide fine control of speed and memory use.
stations.challenge: Give a language choice AND a reason for a school revision app.

tasks.q: A school wants a revision app that staff can update easily. Which justification is strongest?
a: A high-level language makes the code easier to read and maintain
A high-level language guarantees the app uses no memory
Machine code is always easiest for staff to edit
Low-level code automatically works on all devices
tasks.fb: The requirement is easy maintenance. Link your reason to that requirement, rather than making absolute claims.

tasks.q: Select TWO sensible conclusions when choosing a language.
opts: Development time matters as well as execution speed
Different parts of a system can use different language levels
Low-level code is always the best choice
A high-level program never needs translation
correct: Development time matters as well as execution speed
Different parts of a system can use different language levels
tasks.fb: There is no best level for every project. Teams balance development effort, portability and hardware control.

stations.answer: A high-level language supports readable, maintainable code, making updates easier.
stations.info: For a stronger answer, name the requirement, choose the level, then explain how its characteristic meets that requirement.

final.q: Choose the best fit for each brief, using the stated priority.
items: A revision app: readable code and frequent updates
A tiny hardware routine: direct register control
A data report: rapid development using libraries
A processor-specific routine: fine control over instructions
final.fb: Use the priority in each brief. High-level code supports productive development; low-level code supports detailed hardware control.

final.q: Finish the recommendation by matching each choice to its reason.
pairs: High-level for a changing school quiz
Check before moving high-level source to another system
A compatible runtime and dependencies are available
final.fb: An exam explanation should connect a language characteristic to the requirement in the question.

final_answer: Revision app and data report: high-level. Processor-specific routines: low-level. Link readability to maintenance, hardware operations to direct control, and portability to a compatible runtime.
plenary: Explain two benefits of a high-level language for staff maintaining a school quiz app. [4]
Readable source is easier for staff to understand.
That makes updates easier to maintain.
Useful libraries can provide existing functions.
This reduces the amount of code staff need to develop.
State one difference between assembly and machine code. [2]
Assembly uses readable mnemonics for instructions.
Machine code represents processor instructions in binary.
A Python program is moved to another computer. Explain one software requirement before it can run. [2]
The computer needs a compatible Python interpreter or runtime.
It executes the Python source, which the CPU cannot execute directly.

title: Instruction workshop
mission: Trace a small teaching computer, explain what each instruction changes and repair a faulty program.
donow: How can a short instruction make a processor change a stored value?
outcomes: Trace simple input, storage and calculation instructions.
starter: A box contains 6. Add 5, store the result, then subtract 2. What is in the box before and after the subtraction?
starter_answer: Before subtraction: 11. After subtraction: 9. Each instruction uses the result left by the previous one.
terms: Mnemonic
A short name that represents an instruction, such as ADD.
Accumulator
A register that holds a value being processed in this teaching computer.

stations.name: The teaching computer
facts: An accumulator holds the current working value.
Named memory locations store values for later use.
Instructions run in order unless a branch changes the route.
stations.challenge: How is the accumulator different from a memory location?
stations.answer: The accumulator holds the current working value. Memory keeps values that the program can load later.

tasks.q: The accumulator holds 6 and BOX holds 12. Where is the current working value?
tasks.fb: The accumulator is the working register in this model.

tasks.q: Match each part to its role.
pairs: Tells the model what to do
tasks.fb: A register, a memory location and an instruction have different roles.

stations.info: This is a simplified teaching model. Tracing its instructions develops understanding of low-level operations. These mnemonics are not a required OCR J277 instruction list.

stations.name: Input and output
facts: INP places the next input in the accumulator.
OUT displays the accumulator without clearing it.
HLT stops the program.
stations.challenge: Predict the output when the input is 9.
stations.answer: The output is 9. INP reads it, OUT displays it, then HLT stops the program.

tasks.q: INP reads 9. OUT runs next. What is displayed?
tasks.fb: OUT displays the accumulator value, which is 9.

tasks.q: What does HLT do in this model?
tasks.fb: HLT ends the program. OUT displays a value but does not stop the program.

stations.info: Read input values in the order supplied. Two INP instructions consume two inputs, even when both use the same accumulator.

stations.name: Keeping a value
facts: STA copies the accumulator into a named memory location.
LDA copies a stored value into the accumulator.
Loading a value does not remove it from memory.
stations.challenge: After this sequence, what do ACC and BOX contain?
stations.answer: ACC contains 8 and BOX contains 8. The later LDA restores the first input from BOX.

tasks.q: After INP 8, STA BOX, INP 3 and LDA BOX, what is in the accumulator?
tasks.fb: STA saved 8 before the second input. LDA copies that saved value back.

tasks.q: Select TWO true statements about this trace.
opts: BOX still contains 8 after LDA BOX
LDA deletes BOX
The second INP replaces the working value
STA always resets the accumulator to zero
correct: BOX still contains 8 after LDA BOX
The second INP replaces the working value
tasks.fb: Stores and loads copy values. Neither operation here deletes the stored value.

stations.info: The names ACC and BOX are labels for the diagram. BOX represents a memory location, not another accumulator.

stations.name: Calculating step by step
facts: ADD adds a stored value to the accumulator.
SUB subtracts a stored value from the accumulator.
Record each new working value when tracing.
stations.challenge: What does this program output? Show the intermediate values.
stations.answer: LDA gives 8. ADD gives 13. SUB gives 11. OUT displays 11.

tasks.q: Match each instruction to the accumulator value after it runs.
tasks.fb: Trace one instruction at a time: 8, then 13, then 11.

tasks.q: Does ADD B change the value stored at B?
tasks.fb: ADD reads B and updates the accumulator. B stays unchanged.

stations.info: For this model, examples use small non-negative integers. Overflow and a particular real processor encoding are outside these activities.

stations.name: Repairing a program
facts: An input overwrites the accumulator.
Save a value before reading another one if you still need it.
Test a repair with inputs whose sum you can predict.
stations.challenge: Repair the missing instruction so inputs 6 and 4 produce 10.
stations.answer: Insert STA FIRST after the first INP. FIRST then holds 6, so ADD FIRST adds it to the second input 4.

tasks.q: Which instruction belongs in the gap?
tasks.fb: Store the first input before the second input overwrites the accumulator.

tasks.q: If FIRST starts at 0 and the store is missing, what do inputs 6 then 4 produce?
tasks.fb: The second input leaves 4 in the accumulator. Adding the unchanged FIRST value 0 still gives 4.

stations.info: A program may run without reporting an error and still produce the wrong answer. Compare actual output with a predicted result.

stations.name: Linking code to hardware
facts: Assembly uses readable instruction names.
Machine code encodes instructions as binary.
An assembler translates assembly source into machine code.
stations.challenge: Why does readable assembly still count as low-level?
stations.answer: Its operations closely match a processor instruction set and expose hardware details.

tasks.q: Classify these descriptions.
tasks.fb: Assembly and machine code are both low-level. Their representations differ.

tasks.q: What must happen before a real CPU executes assembly source?
a: It must be translated to compatible machine code
It must be converted into a worksheet
tasks.fb: An assembler performs this translation. The teaching computer helps illustrate the idea.

stations.info: The assembler is included to explain this practical activity. The main assessed translator comparison in J277 is compiler versus interpreter.

final.q: For inputs 7 and 2, match each point to the working value.
final.fb: Store the first value, read the second, then add the saved first value.

final.q: Which test best checks that the repaired program adds both inputs?
a: Check that the source file opens
Check that OUT is written in capitals
final.fb: Different non-zero inputs reveal whether one value was lost.

final_answer: INP 7 leaves 7. STA FIRST stores 7 and leaves ACC at 7. INP 2 leaves 2. ADD FIRST makes 9. OUT displays 9.
plenary: Explain the difference between assembly and machine code. [2]
Assembly uses mnemonic instruction names.
Machine code uses binary instructions a compatible CPU executes.
A program reads two inputs into one accumulator. Explain why it must store the first before reading the second if it needs both. [2]
The second input replaces the accumulator value.
Storing the first preserves it for later use.
Trace LDA X, ADD Y, SUB Z, OUT for X = 9, Y = 4 and Z = 3. Give the intermediate values and output. [4]
After LDA X: 9.
After ADD Y: 13.
After SUB Z: 10.
OUT displays 10.

title: Translation studio
mission: Follow source code through translation and choose a compiler or interpreter for different working situations.
donow: Why can a CPU not simply follow a Python source file as written?
outcomes: Compare how compilers and interpreters work.
Justify a translator choice using the task requirements.
starter: A programmer writes total = price * quantity. Identify the source code and explain why the CPU needs another representation.
starter_answer: The written statement is source code. The CPU executes instructions in its own machine-code instruction set.
terms: Compiler
A translator that processes a program into target code before that translated program runs.
Interpreter
Software that translates and executes source instructions as the program runs.

stations.name: Why translate?
facts: Source code expresses a program in a human-readable language.
A CPU executes compatible machine instructions.
A translator connects the source language to execution.
stations.challenge: Why is saving a source file not enough to make it executable by a CPU?
stations.answer: Saving keeps the source text. It does not itself translate the program into instructions the CPU can execute.

tasks.q: Why does high-level source need translation?
a: The CPU executes machine instructions, not high-level source directly
The CPU can only process images
tasks.fb: Translation changes representation. It does not prove the algorithm correct.

tasks.q: Match each item to its meaning.
pairs: Software that processes one code form into another
tasks.fb: Separate the program representation from the software that translates it.

stations.info: Real language implementations can mix techniques. This lesson uses the GCSE comparison of compilation before execution and interpretation during execution.

stations.name: The compiler route
facts: A compiler processes the source program before execution.
It reports translation errors it finds.
A successful build can produce code that is run later.
stations.challenge: Why might compilation suit software used repeatedly by customers?
stations.answer: Users can run the translated program repeatedly without translating the whole source again each time.

tasks.q: In the usual GCSE model, when does compilation happen?
a: Before the translated program is executed
Only after every run has finished
Only when the source is printed
tasks.fb: Compilation produces target code before that translated program runs.

tasks.q: Place each action in the build or run stage.
tasks.fb: A build creates translated code. Running executes it.

stations.info: Object code may need linking with other code before it becomes a complete executable. A compiler does not always produce a ready-to-run file in one step.

stations.name: The interpreter route
facts: An interpreter processes source instructions as they execute.
It typically stops when it encounters an error it cannot handle.
The usual GCSE model has no separate standalone executable.
stations.challenge: Why can an interpreter help during short edit-and-test cycles?
stations.answer: The programmer can edit source and test it without a separate whole-program compilation step.

tasks.q: Which best describes interpretation in the GCSE model?
a: Translate and execute instructions during the run
Translate the whole program once and discard the source
tasks.fb: Interpretation combines translation and execution during a run.

tasks.q: An unhandled error occurs during an interpreted run. What normally happens?
a: Execution stops and an error is reported
The source becomes machine code permanently
Every later instruction must still run
tasks.fb: Earlier instructions may already have run before the error is encountered.

stations.info: An interpreter may internally use bytecode or other processing. “One instruction at a time” is a teaching comparison, not a rule for every implementation.

stations.name: Errors at different stages
facts: Translation can reveal some syntax errors.
A program can translate successfully and still contain logic errors.
Testing checks whether outputs meet the requirements.
stations.challenge: A compiled program gives the wrong discount. Has translation proved it correct?
stations.answer: No. The code can obey syntax rules while implementing the wrong calculation. Test its outputs against expected results.

tasks.q: Which kind of issue is described?
items: A missing bracket breaks the language rules
A valid formula applies the wrong discount
A loop runs one time too many
tasks.fb: Syntax concerns language rules. Logic concerns whether valid instructions solve the intended problem.

tasks.q: What does a successful compilation prove?
a: The compiler accepted the source for translation
tasks.fb: Successful translation is useful but does not establish correctness.

stations.info: An error message often points to where a problem was noticed. The actual cause can be on an earlier line.

stations.name: Time and distribution
facts: Compilation takes time before the translated program runs.
Built programs can run without the original compiler installed.
Interpreted source normally needs a compatible interpreter or runtime.
stations.challenge: A user has a compiled executable. Must they install the original compiler?
stations.answer: Usually no. They need a compatible system and any required runtime libraries, but not the original compiler.

tasks.q: Select TWO sensible comparisons.
opts: Compilation adds a build step
Compiled software never needs libraries
Interpreted source needs suitable execution software
An interpreter guarantees faster execution
correct: Interpreted source needs suitable execution software
tasks.fb: Consider the build step and the target environment. Avoid absolute speed claims.

tasks.q: What may be needed when compiled software moves to a different processor architecture?
a: A compatible build for that architecture
tasks.fb: Machine code targets an instruction set. Compatibility matters.

stations.info: Compiled code is often faster to run in the simplified comparison because source translation has already happened. Actual performance depends on the implementation and program.

stations.name: Choosing a route
facts: Frequent edits can favour an interpreter during development.
Repeated distribution can favour a compiled build.
Give a reason linked to the stated requirement.
stations.challenge: Choose a route for a developer testing small changes frequently and explain your choice.
stations.answer: An interpreter supports quick edit-and-run cycles without a separate full compilation step.

tasks.q: A developer is testing many small changes. Which is a sound reason for using an interpreter?
a: It always hides the source code
It requires no software on the computer
tasks.fb: Link the choice to the work being done, not an absolute promise.

tasks.q: A team supplies a built application to users. Which compiler benefit fits?
a: Users can run the translated program without the original compiler
The program can never contain bugs
tasks.fb: The build separates translation from use. Compatibility and testing still matter.

stations.info: Many teams use both approaches in different parts of their workflow. A GCSE recommendation should use the requirements in the question.

final.q: Match the situation to the explanation.
pairs: Quickly retest a changed source statement
Run a finished program many times
A compiled build avoids repeating source translation
A translated program gives the wrong answer
final.fb: Choose using the requirement and explain the relevant characteristic.

final.q: Select TWO claims you can defend.
opts: Translation does not replace testing
Every interpreter is faster than every compiler
A compiled program may need a compatible runtime library
Successful compilation guarantees correct outputs
correct: A compiled program may need a compatible runtime library
final.fb: Neither translator type guarantees correct behaviour or universal compatibility.

final_answer: Quick retesting: interpreter. Repeated use of a finished build: compiler. Wrong results after successful translation: test and repair the logic.
plenary: State why a high-level program needs a translator. [2]
The CPU executes machine code.
The translator processes high-level source into a form that can be executed.
Describe two differences between a compiler and an interpreter in the GCSE model. [4]
A compiler translates the source program before execution.
An interpreter translates and executes instructions during execution.
A compiled build can run again without retranslating the source each time.
Interpretation requires the interpreter or suitable runtime when running the source.
A program compiles but calculates tax incorrectly. Explain why testing is still needed. [2]
The program may contain a logic error despite valid syntax.
Testing compares actual results with expected results to identify the fault.

title: IDE control room
mission: Use an editor, execution tools and debugging information to find faults and explain how an IDE supports programming.
donow: What help would you want from the software you use to write programs?
outcomes: Explain how editing and diagnostics support programmers.
Use a breakpoint, stepping and variable values to investigate a fault.
starter: A program runs but calculates 3 + 4 as 34. Suggest a cause and one useful piece of evidence to inspect.
starter_answer: The inputs may be strings, so + joins them. Inspect the types and values of the inputs before the calculation.
terms: IDE
An integrated development environment brings programming tools together in one application.
Breakpoint
A chosen point where a debugger pauses execution for inspection.

stations.name: Tools in one place
facts: IDE means integrated development environment.
An IDE combines tools used to create and test programs.
Its facilities may include editing, execution and debugging.
stations.challenge: Why can bringing these tools together help a programmer?
stations.answer: The programmer can edit, run and investigate code in one place, reducing switching between separate tools.

tasks.q: What is an IDE?
a: An application that brings programming tools together
tasks.fb: The IDE supports programming. It is not itself the source language.

tasks.q: Match each facility to its purpose.
tasks.fb: These facilities work together within the development environment.

stations.info: Different IDEs provide different tools. An editor can be part of an IDE, but a simple text editor alone may not include execution or debugging.

stations.name: Writing source code
facts: Syntax highlighting uses colour to distinguish code elements.
Auto-completion suggests names or code as you type.
Indentation tools help present blocks clearly.
stations.challenge: How can auto-completion reduce mistakes without guaranteeing correct code?
stations.answer: It can reduce typing errors in suggested names, but the programmer can still select the wrong name or write the wrong logic.

tasks.q: Match the editor feature to the benefit.
pairs: Makes code elements easier to distinguish
tasks.fb: Editing support improves productivity and readability, but programmers still need to check their code.

tasks.q: Does syntax highlighting prove that a calculation is correct?
a: No, it mainly helps distinguish code elements
Yes, all coloured code is correct
Yes, if every line is blue
Only when the font is large
tasks.fb: Colour is a reading aid. It does not prove the algorithm gives the intended result.

stations.info: Colour meanings vary between themes and IDEs. Recognise what highlighting does rather than memorising one colour scheme.

stations.name: Translation and execution
facts: An IDE can call a compiler or interpreter.
Run controls start the program using its configured tools.
The output area shows results and may accept input.
stations.challenge: What is the difference between the editor and the output area?
stations.answer: The editor contains the source being written. The output area shows what happens when the program runs.

tasks.q: Which facility lets you start the program and see its output?
tasks.fb: The IDE invokes its configured execution tools and displays the results.

tasks.q: Where would you look to see the result of print(6 * 4)?
tasks.fb: The statement sends 24 to the output area.

stations.info: An IDE may require a separately installed compiler or interpreter. The interface and the language execution tool have different jobs.

stations.name: Diagnostic messages
facts: Diagnostics identify detected problems in the code.
A message can include a line number and an error description.
Read the surrounding code before deciding on a repair.
stations.challenge: A message points to line 5. Why might you also inspect line 4?
stations.answer: An earlier missing bracket or other error may only become apparent when the tool reaches the next line.

tasks.q: Which repair addresses the visible syntax error on line 4?
a: Add the closing ) after the string
tasks.fb: The opening bracket needs a matching closing bracket.

tasks.q: Select TWO sensible uses of diagnostics.
opts: Read the message to identify the kind of problem
Assume the IDE repairs every fault automatically
Inspect nearby lines as well as the highlighted one
Ignore testing once the message disappears
correct: Read the message to identify the kind of problem
Inspect nearby lines as well as the highlighted one
tasks.fb: Diagnostics guide investigation. The reported location may be where a problem was noticed.

stations.info: A warning can differ from an error that prevents execution. Read the message rather than treating every highlight as the same kind of problem.

stations.name: Pausing and stepping
facts: A breakpoint pauses before a selected line executes.
Step controls advance execution in small steps.
Watching variables reveals how values change.
stations.challenge: If execution pauses before total = price * quantity, what can you inspect first?
stations.answer: Inspect the current values of price and quantity. Step over the calculation, then inspect total.

tasks.q: Execution pauses before the calculation. What should you do to inspect its result?
a: Step over it, then inspect total
tasks.fb: A breakpoint pauses before the line. Stepping lets you see the effect of executing it.

tasks.q: Match the debugging action to its use.
pairs: Execute a line and pause again
tasks.fb: Use the facilities together to investigate where actual behaviour diverges from your expectation.

stations.info: Stepping options differ. Step into can enter a called function, while step over runs that call without stopping on each line inside it.

stations.name: Finding a logic error
facts: A logic error can remain even when syntax is valid.
Compare actual values with the result you expected.
Retest after changing the faulty statement.
stations.challenge: The bill should be 24 but is 10. Identify and repair the calculation.
stations.answer: Replace price + quantity with price * quantity. Test that 6 and 4 produce 24, then try another case.

tasks.q: Which replacement meets the stated requirement?
tasks.fb: Multiplying the unit price by the quantity calculates the bill.

tasks.q: Which is the strongest follow-up after the repair?
a: Run the original test and another known case
Assume one edit fixed every possible fault
Check only that the source is coloured
tasks.fb: Retesting checks the repair. More than one known case gives better evidence.

stations.info: Debugging finds and fixes faults. Testing supplies evidence about whether the program meets its requirements.

final.q: Select the useful IDE facility for each need.
pairs: Reduce typing of a long variable name
Stop just before an incorrect calculation
See a message about a missing bracket
final.fb: Choose the facility that directly addresses the programmer’s next step.

final.q: A debugger shows correct inputs but the wrong result after one line. What should happen next?
a: Inspect that calculation, repair it and retest
Assume the debugger caused the fault
final.fb: The evidence narrows the investigation to the calculation.

final_answer: Auto-completion helps with typing. Breakpoints pause at a chosen line. Watches display values. Diagnostics describe detected problems. Use this evidence to repair and retest.
plenary: Name two IDE editing facilities and explain how each helps a programmer. [4]
Syntax highlighting makes code elements easier to distinguish.
Auto-completion suggests names and can reduce typing errors.
Award one mark for each facility and one for its explained benefit.
Automatic indentation with a clear benefit is also acceptable.
Explain how a breakpoint and a variable watch can help investigate a wrong total. [2]
A breakpoint pauses near the calculation.
The variable watch shows values to compare with the expected inputs or result.
Why must a programmer still test code after all syntax errors have been corrected? [2]
Valid syntax can still express incorrect logic.
Testing checks actual results against expected results.

title: Language review HQ
mission: Apply the whole topic to short scenarios, check your reasoning and use review mode to repair misunderstandings.
donow: Which tool or language choice would most help you build a reliable revision app?
outcomes: Recall language levels and translator behaviour.
Select IDE tools for specific problems.
Write explanations linked to the needs of a scenario.
starter: A quiz app runs successfully but awards every answer a mark. Is this evidence that the logic is correct? Explain.
starter_answer: No. Running without an error does not prove the rules are correct. Test correct and incorrect answers against expected scores.
terms: Source code
The program text written by a programmer before translation.
Logic error
A mistake in a program’s reasoning that causes incorrect behaviour.

stations.name: Language decisions
facts: High-level languages hide many hardware details.
Low-level languages expose processor operations.
The project requirements should guide the choice.
stations.challenge: Choose a level for a school app that needs frequent updates. Explain why.
stations.answer: High-level code is usually easier to read and maintain, helping staff update the app.

tasks.q: Choose the level that fits the priority.
tasks.fb: Link the language characteristic to the priority in the brief.

tasks.q: Why is “low-level is always better” a weak recommendation?
a: It ignores the requirements and development trade-offs
Every task needs machine code written by hand
tasks.fb: Different priorities lead to different language choices.

stations.info: A strong explanation names a characteristic and shows how it meets a requirement. A language name alone is often not enough.

stations.name: Representations
facts: Source code is the programmer’s representation.
Assembly uses mnemonic instructions.
Machine code contains encoded processor instructions.
stations.challenge: Explain why assembly and machine code are both low-level.
stations.answer: Both closely relate to a processor instruction set, even though assembly uses readable mnemonics.

tasks.q: Match each description.
pairs: ADD as a readable instruction name
tasks.fb: Source code can be high-level or assembly. Machine code is executable by a compatible processor.

tasks.q: Which representation does a compatible CPU execute directly?
tasks.fb: The processor recognises instructions from its machine-code instruction set.

stations.info: The same binary sequence need not mean the same instruction on another architecture. Compatibility cannot be assumed.

stations.name: Translator choices
facts: Compilers process source before the translated program runs.
Interpreters process source during execution.
Neither approach removes the need to test.
stations.challenge: Which route supports quick testing of frequent source edits? Why?
stations.answer: An interpreter supports quick edit-and-run cycles without a separate whole-program compilation step.

tasks.q: Use the usual GCSE translator comparison.
items: Translate before executing the built program
Produce target code for later use
Use source with an execution runtime
tasks.fb: These are the simplified GCSE models. Real implementations can combine techniques.

tasks.q: A compiled app gives the wrong output. What is the best conclusion?
a: It may contain a logic error that testing can reveal
Compilers always ignore every syntax error
The output must be correct because it compiled
tasks.fb: Successful translation does not prove that the program meets its requirements.

stations.info: When comparing two approaches, make paired points. Explain what each does rather than listing unrelated advantages.

stations.name: IDE evidence
facts: Editor features help create readable source.
Diagnostics report detected problems.
Debugging tools help inspect execution.
stations.challenge: Which tools would help you find why a total changes incorrectly?
stations.answer: Pause before the calculation with a breakpoint, inspect inputs, step over the line and inspect the total.

tasks.q: Choose the tool for the job.
pairs: Suggest a variable name while typing
tasks.fb: Use each tool for its specific purpose.

tasks.q: Which feature mainly makes keywords and strings easier to distinguish?
tasks.fb: Syntax highlighting changes the display of code elements, not the program logic.

stations.info: The IDE offers facilities. The programmer uses their evidence to decide what change to make.

stations.name: Interpreting a trace
facts: A trace records the effect of each instruction.
Stored values and the working value are different.
Predict before checking the result.
stations.challenge: Trace 5 + 8, then subtract 4. What are the two results?
stations.answer: After addition: 13. After subtraction: 9.

tasks.q: What is the working value after adding 8 to 5?
tasks.fb: Both values are numeric. Addition gives 13.

tasks.q: What is output after subtracting 4 from that result?
tasks.fb: 13 minus 4 is 9. Follow the updated working value.

stations.info: The arithmetic trace applies the idea of instruction order. You do not need to memorise an extra assembly instruction set for J277.

stations.name: Writing an explanation
facts: Read the requirement before choosing a feature.
Name a relevant characteristic.
Explain its effect on the stated problem.
stations.challenge: Improve “Use an IDE because it is good” with one specific example.
stations.answer: Use a breakpoint to pause near the faulty calculation, then inspect variable values to locate the error.

tasks.q: Which response best explains an IDE benefit for investigating a wrong answer?
a: A breakpoint pauses near the calculation so variable values can be checked
An IDE is useful because it is modern
An IDE makes every program correct
An IDE is a type of CPU
tasks.fb: The first response connects a feature to how it helps solve the problem.

tasks.q: Select TWO habits that strengthen an exam explanation.
opts: Use a specific feature or characteristic
Repeat the question without adding a reason
Link its effect to the scenario
Use “always” for every comparison
correct: Use a specific feature or characteristic
Link its effect to the scenario
tasks.fb: Specific, linked points explain more than vague praise or unsupported absolutes.

stations.info: Use the marks as a guide to the number of distinct points. Correct terminology helps, but the link to the scenario matters too.

final.q: Recommend a tool or approach for each priority.
pairs: Pause before a suspected faulty line
Execute instructions directly on a compatible CPU
final.fb: Explain the benefit of each recommendation in the context given.

opts: Successful translation does not guarantee correct logic
Every IDE automatically repairs every program
Hardware compatibility matters for machine code
High-level source always runs unchanged anywhere
correct: Successful translation does not guarantee correct logic
Hardware compatibility matters for machine code
final.fb: Testing and compatibility remain important regardless of the development tools.

final_answer: Frequent source edits: interpreter. Maintainable app: high-level language. Pause near a fault: breakpoint. Direct CPU execution: machine code.
plenary: A school will update its quiz app each week. Explain two reasons for choosing a high-level language. [4]
Readable source helps staff understand the program.
This makes frequent changes easier to maintain.
Useful libraries can reduce how much code staff must write.
This can reduce development time for new features.
Compare a compiler and an interpreter. [4]
A compiler translates before the resulting program runs.
An interpreter processes source during execution.
Compiled target code can be run again without repeating source translation.
Interpreted source requires its interpreter or execution runtime.
A bill is wrong even though the program runs. Explain how two IDE debugging facilities could help. [4]
A breakpoint pauses execution near the calculation.
This allows inspection before or after the suspected operation.
A variable watch shows current input or result values.
Comparing these with expected values helps locate the fault.
